fields.claim_quote: However, a minimal cut in a subgraph like G[A] or G[B] is also a minimal cut in the entire graph G.
fields.complete_source:
Solution
Proof. Let G be an undirected graph. An edge cut (or simply cut) in G is any set E of
edges whose removal disconnects G (i.e. G −E has more connected components than
G). A cut E is called minimal (also known as a bond) if no proper subset of E is itself
a cut. Equivalently, E is minimal if removing any strictly smaller set of edges fails to
disconnect G. We will prove that any cut E in G can be expressed as a disjoint union of
minimal cuts.
We proceed by induction on |E|, the number of edges in the cut.
**Base Case:** If |E| = 1, then E consists of a single edge. Removing one edge
disconnects G only if that edge is a bridge, in which case E is already a minimal cut. So
the statement holds trivially for |E| = 1. (If a single edge removal did not disconnect G,
then E would not be a cut in the first place.)
**Inductive Step:** Now assume the statement holds for all cuts with fewer than m
edges, and let E be any cut with |E| = m ≥2. We distinguish two cases:
1. **E is already a minimal cut:** In this case, E itself is one of the minimal cut
components, and we can simply express E as the union of the single minimal cut E (the
union of one set being itself). Thus the claim holds (trivially) for E.
2. **E is not a minimal cut:** Then by definition, there exists a proper subset E′ ⊊E
that is also a cut of G. Among all cut-subsets of E, choose one that is inclusion-wise
minimal (i.e. choose F ⊊E such that F is a cut and no proper subset of F is a cut).
Such an F exists because E itself is finite and not minimal, so we can remove edges from
E one by one until reaching a minimal cut. Let this minimal cut be F. By construction,
F is a minimal cut (bond) of G, and F ̸= E (since E is not minimal).
Remove the edges F from G. Since F is a cut, G−F is disconnected. In fact, because
F is minimal, removing F splits G into exactly two connected components. (If G −F
had more than two components, then some proper subset of F would already disconnect
one part of G, contradicting the minimality of F.) Let A and B be the vertex-sets of
these two components of G −F. Thus F consists precisely of all edges in G that had one
endpoint in A and the other endpoint in B. We now examine the remaining edges E \ F,
which we have not yet removed.
Every edge in E \ F lies entirely within one of the two components A or B. Indeed,
if some e ∈E \ F had one endpoint in A and one in B, then e would belong to F (since
F removed all A-B connections). Therefore we can partition
E \ F = EA ∪EB,
where EA denotes those edges of E \ F with both endpoints in A, and EB are those with
both endpoints in B. (By construction EA and EB are disjoint, and EA ∪EB = E \ F.)
Now observe that EA is an edge cut within the subgraph G[A] induced by A. This
is because in the original graph G, removing all of E = F ∪EA ∪EB disconnected G
completely. We have already removed F (which separated A from B); further removing
EA will disconnect the component A itself into smaller pieces (since EA were edges in
A whose removal was necessary to break all connectivity inside A).
In other words,
G[A] −EA is disconnected. Hence EA is a cut in the subgraph G[A]. Similarly, EB is a
cut in the subgraph G[B] (as G[B] −EB is disconnected).
Note that |EA| < |E| and |EB| < |E| (indeed |EA| + |EB| = |E \ F| = |E| −|F|, and
|F| ≥1). We can now apply the induction hypothesis to each of these smaller cuts: by

the inductive assumption, EA can be expressed as a disjoint union of minimal cuts (within
G[A]), and EB can be expressed as a disjoint union of minimal cuts (within G[B]).
However, a minimal cut in a subgraph like G[A] or G[B] is also a minimal cut in
the entire graph G. To see this, consider any minimal cut HA ⊆EA in the subgraph
G[A]. Since HA is a cut in G[A], removing HA disconnects A (in the subgraph). But
HA ⊆EA ⊆E, so none of the edges in HA go between A and B. This means that if we
remove HA in the full graph G, the vertices in A become disconnected among themselves
(just as in G[A]), and of course they remain disconnected from B as well (since F is
already removed when considering the context of G[A]). Thus HA disconnects G, so HA
is a cut in G. Moreover, HA was minimal in G[A], meaning no subset of HA disconnects
A; in G, any subset of HA would certainly fail to disconnect G (since it wouldn’t even
disconnect A), so HA is minimal in G as well. By the same reasoning, any minimal cut
HB ⊆EB in G[B] is also a minimal cut in G.
Therefore, combining everything: we have written
EA = HA,1 ∪HA,2 ∪· · · ∪HA,p,
EB = HB,1 ∪HB,2 ∪· · · ∪HB,q,
where each HA,i and each HB,j is a minimal cut (bond) in G. These unions are disjoint
unions (each HA,i is disjoint from HA,j, etc., and similarly for B-side), and also EA is
disjoint from EB by construction. Now recall that E = F ∪EA ∪EB, with F a minimal
cut as well. Moreover, F, EA, and EB are pairwise disjoint sets of edges. It follows that

fields.explanation: Keep the four-cycle x-y-u-v-x, E all four edges, F={yu,vx}, A={x,y}, B={u,v}, and HA={xy}. F is a proper minimal cut and HA is the entire remaining A-edge cut. Deleting HA from the original graph leaves the connected path x-v-u-y. The theorem proves actual SimpleGraph connectivity, minimum cut F under all proper subsets, exact reachability characterization of A after deleting F, minimum cut HA in the actual induced subgraph, and that deleting HA from G is connected. This removes the unproved fixed-depth component computations.
fields.flaw: A minimal cut in an induced subgraph G[A] or G[B] obtained after removing F is also a minimal cut in the entire graph G.

Problem Statement
Problem: Algorithms - 33
Let G be an undirected graph. Demonstrate that every cut in G can be expressed as the
disjoint union of minimal cuts.

fields.witness:
4-cycle; F={xv,yu}; H_A={xy} cuts G[A] but G−xy connected

Use the 4-cycle x-y-u-v-x. Let E be all four edges, i.e. delta({x,u}). Choose F={xv,yu}, a minimal cut; then G-F has components A={x,y} and B={u,v}. In G[A], HA={xy} is a minimal cut. But in the full graph G, deleting xy leaves the path x-v-u-y, so G-HA is connected. Thus HA is not even a cut in G.
